t: That the last sentence of section 13(b) of the Civil Service Retirement Act, 5 U.S.C. 2263(b), is amended to read as follows: “Notwithstanding the restriction contained in section 115 of the Social Security Amendments of 1954, Public. Law 83–761, a similar right to redetermination after deposit shall be applicable to an annuitant (1) whose annuity is based on an involuntary separation from the service and (2) who is separated on or after July 12, 1960, after such period of full-time reemployment which began before October 1, 1956.”

fable.w: This section amends the Civil Service Retirement Act to extend a right to annuity redetermination to certain reemployed annuitants, which is a benefit entitlement rather than a consultative process. The word "right" might suggest a right to challenge a federal decision, but it is only a right to have a benefit recomputed after a deposit. No outside party is consulted, heard, or given a right to sue or object to a federal decision.
fable.s: a similar right to redetermination after deposit shall be applicable to an annuitant

qwen_block.w: This section amends a statute to grant a specific right to redetermination of annuity benefits to certain federal employees. It does not involve consultation, coordination, or participation by outside parties in a federal decision-making process. The text describes eligibility criteria for a benefit, which falls under the exclusion for applications for benefits or grants.
qwen_block.s: That the last sentence of section 13(b) of the Civil Service Retirement Act, 5 U.S.C. 2263(b), is amended to read as follows: “Notwithstanding the restriction contained in section 115 of the Social Security Amendments of 1954, Public. Law 83–761, a similar right to redetermination after deposit shall be applicable to an annuitant (1) whose annuity is based on an involuntary separation from the service and (2) who is separated on or after July 12, 1960, after such period of full-time reemployment which began before October 1, 1956.”

opus.w: This amendment extends an annuitant's right to have their own civil service retirement annuity recalculated after making a deposit. That is a claim for an individual benefit, which the definition excludes. It is not a comment period, hearing, advisory body, consultation, or right to sue over a federal decision. The 'right to redetermination' may sound like a right to object, but it only adjusts a personal benefit amount.
opus.s: a similar right to redetermination after deposit shall be applicable to an annuitant (1) whose annuity is based on an involuntary separation from the service
opus.b: The tempting reading is that "a similar right to redetermination" lets an outside party challenge a federal decision. That doesn't hold up. The redetermination is a recalculation of an individual annuitant's own retirement annuity after the annuitant makes a deposit. That is a benefit claim, which the definition excludes, not a role in a federal policy decision.

qwen_chat.w: This section amends the eligibility criteria for the recalculation of a federal employee's pension. It does not require consultation with outside parties, public comment, or advisory committees. The definition explicitly excludes applications for benefits or grants, and this provision falls squarely within that exclusion as it pertains to the calculation of individual benefits rather than participatory decision-making.
qwen_chat.s: a similar right to redetermination after deposit shall be applicable to an annuitant (1) whose annuity is based on an involuntary separation from the service and (2) who is separated on or after July 12, 1960, after such period of full-time reemployment which began before October 1, 1956.
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that "redetermination" implies a process where the individual participates in deciding their benefit status. However, the definition explicitly excludes "applications for benefits or grants." This section merely amends the eligibility criteria for a specific administrative recalculation of a pension; it does not establish a mechanism for outside parties to consult with the government on policy decisions, nor does it grant a right to sue or participate in rulemaking. It is a substantive change to benefit rules, not a procedural participation requirement.
